q: Which mixture needs fractional distillation rather than simple distillation to separate it?
options: two miscible liquids with similar boiling points
an insoluble solid in a liquid
explain: Fractional distillation is used for liquids that mix and whose boiling points are close, so one distillation does not separate them. The other mixtures need filtration, simple distillation or chromatography.

q: During the fractional distillation of a mixture of two miscible liquids, what happens to the thermometer reading at the top of the column?
options: It rises steadily all the time.
It stays steady at the boiling point of the lower boiling liquid, then rises.
It falls as the first liquid distils.
It stays at the boiling point of the higher boiling liquid.
explain: While the more volatile liquid distils the temperature stays near its boiling point. When it has gone, the temperature rises towards the boiling point of the other liquid.

q: Crystals are filtered from a solution and washed with a small amount of cold distilled water. Why is only a small amount of cold water used?
options: to remove soluble impurities without dissolving much of the crystals
explain: The washing water removes solution clinging to the crystals. Using little and cold water means that only a small amount of the crystals dissolve.

q: A saturated solution of a salt is cooled from 80 °C to 20 °C and crystals form. Why?
options: The salt reacts with the water at 20 °C.
Water evaporates when the solution is cooled.
The solubility of the salt is lower at the lower temperature, so the excess solute comes out of solution.
explain: Most salts are less soluble when cold. The solution holds too much solute at 20 °C, so the excess crystallises.

q: A fermented mixture contains yeast cells (insoluble), ethanol and water. Which sequence best obtains ethanol?
options: filtration to remove the yeast, then fractional distillation
explain: Filtration removes the insoluble yeast. The ethanol and water are miscible liquids with different boiling points, so fractional distillation separates them.

q: While a liquid is boiling, the thermometer reading stays constant at 78 °C. What does this suggest about the liquid?
options: It is a mixture of two liquids.
It is a solid dissolved in water.
It is probably a single pure substance.
explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature. In a mixture the boiling temperature would rise as the more volatile component is lost.

q: Which method gives pure water from seawater?
explain: Simple distillation evaporates the water and condenses it again, leaving the dissolved salts behind.

q: A pure liquid boils sharply at 56 °C. Boiling points: ethanol 78 °C, water 100 °C, propanone 56 °C, hexane 69 °C. Which liquid is it most likely to be?
explain: A pure liquid has a fixed boiling point. The sample matches the boiling point of propanone.

q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a solid. It fizzes, and the gas turns limewater milky. Which ion is most likely to be present in the solid?
explain: Carbonates react with acid to give carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. Sulfates, chlorides and nitrates do not give this gas.

q: Which row gives the colour of the precipitate formed when acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added?
explain: Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.

q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before aqueous silver nitrate when testing for halide ions?
options: to make silver nitrate more soluble
to react with carbonate ions that would also form a precipitate with silver ions
explain: Silver carbonate is also an insoluble precipitate. Adding nitric acid first destroys any carbonate so that only a halide gives a precipitate.

q: A colourless solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and aqueous barium nitrate is added. A white precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
explain: Barium ions form insoluble white barium sulfate. Carbonate would have been destroyed by the acid and chloride and nitrate give no precipitate with barium ions.

q: Why must dilute sulfuric acid not be used to acidify the solution in the test for sulfate ions?
options: It contains sulfate ions, which would give a precipitate with barium ions.
It would react with the barium nitrate to form a gas.
It is too weak an acid to remove carbonate ions.
It would turn the barium nitrate solution acidic.
explain: Sulfuric acid supplies sulfate ions, so a white precipitate would form whether or not the sample contained sulfate. Nitric acid is used instead.

q: Which procedure and observation are correct for the test for nitrate ions?
options: Add dilute acid; carbon dioxide is given off and turns limewater milky.
Add acidified silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms.
Add aluminium foil and dilute acid; hydrogen is given off and burns with a squeaky pop.
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil and warm; ammonia is given off and turns damp red litmus paper blue.
explain: In alkaline solution, aluminium reduces nitrate ions to ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

q: What happens to the nitrate ions in the test with aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
options: They are oxidised to nitrogen dioxide.
They are unchanged; the ammonia comes from the sodium hydroxide.
explain: Aluminium reduces nitrate (nitrogen oxidation state +5) to ammonia (−3). Sodium hydroxide contains no nitrogen, so it cannot be the source of ammonia.

q: A colourless solution decolourises acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), changing from purple to colourless. Which ion could be present?
explain: Sulfite ions reduce the manganate(VII) ions, so the purple colour disappears. Sulfate, carbonate and nitrate do not.

q: A sodium compound fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas turns limewater milky. Which compound could it be?
explain: The gas is carbon dioxide, which comes from the reaction of acid with a carbonate. Sulfates, chlorides and nitrates do not give carbon dioxide.

q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate in the test for chloride ions?
explain: Silver ions and chloride ions combine in a 1 : 1 ratio to give insoluble silver chloride. Silver nitrate and barium chloride are both soluble.

q: Which ionic equation represents the formation of the precipitate in the test for sulfate ions?
explain: One Ba²⁺ ion combines with one SO₄²⁻ ion to give solid BaSO₄, which is insoluble. The charges must balance: +2 and −2.

q: What is seen when aqueous silver nitrate is added to an acidified solution of potassium iodide?
explain: Iodide ions form yellow silver iodide. White is for chloride and cream is for bromide.

q: Which ionic equation represents the reaction between carbonate ions and dilute acid?
explain: Carbonate ions react with hydrogen ions to give carbon dioxide and water. Only this equation balances in both atoms and charge.

q: Which row correctly describes a test for an ion?
options: SO₄²⁻ | acidified aqueous silver nitrate | white precipitate
SO₄²⁻ | acidified aqueous barium nitrate | white precipitate
Cl⁻ | acidified aqueous barium nitrate | white precipitate
CO₃²⁻ | dilute acid | no visible change
explain: Sulfate ions are tested with acidified barium nitrate. Chloride ions need acidified silver nitrate, and carbonates fizz with dilute acid.

q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution until in excess. A light blue precipitate forms which does not dissolve. Which cation is present?
explain: Copper(II) hydroxide is light blue and insoluble in excess alkali. Iron(II) is green, iron(III) is red-brown and chromium(III) is green.

q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a red-brown precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
explain: Fe³⁺ forms red-brown iron(III) hydroxide which is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide.

q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
explain: Fe²⁺ forms a green precipitate that is insoluble in excess. The green precipitate from chromium(III) dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

q: A solution is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. A gas is given off that turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which cation is present?
explain: Ammonium ions react with alkali on warming to release ammonia, the only common alkaline gas, which turns damp red litmus blue.

q: Aqueous aluminium ions and aqueous zinc ions both give a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess. How can the two be distinguished?
options: Add more aqueous sodium hydroxide: only the zinc precipitate dissolves.
Add aqueous ammonia in excess: the aluminium precipitate dissolves but the zinc precipitate does not.
Add dilute nitric acid: only the aluminium precipitate dissolves.
Add aqueous ammonia in excess: the zinc precipitate dissolves but the aluminium precipitate does not.
explain: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution, but aluminium hydroxide stays as a white precipitate.

q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. With aqueous ammonia there is no precipitate or only a very slight one. Which cation is present?
explain: Calcium hydroxide is a white precipitate that is insoluble in excess alkali. Aluminium and zinc precipitates dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, and ammonium gives no precipitate.

q: Excess aqueous ammonia is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. What is seen?
options: A light blue precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
A light blue precipitate forms and then dissolves to give a dark blue solution.
A green precipitate forms and does not dissolve.
explain: Copper(II) hydroxide first forms as a light blue precipitate, which dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep blue solution.

q: Which row correctly describes what happens when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added slowly to excess?
options: Al³⁺ | white precipitate that dissolves in excess
Ca²⁺ | white precipitate that dissolves in excess
Cu²⁺ | blue precipitate that dissolves in excess
Fe³⁺ | green precipitate that does not dissolve in excess
explain: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so its white precipitate dissolves in excess. Calcium hydroxide does not dissolve, copper(II) hydroxide does not dissolve and iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate.
